gaps: Step 7 (what defines 'modern' 2023-2026 dashboard trends and which are usability-grounded vs fad-driven): coverage rests mainly on a single practitioner retrospective (studiomeyer.io) for reasoned analysis, plus several lower-reliability trend-roundup blogs (e.g. orbix.studio) for descriptive corroboration of bento-grid/glassmorphism specifics. Adequate for a durable reference but thinner on independent, evidence-based corroboration than other steps — brief should flag trend claims as more provisional.

Step 6 (generic/templated vs distinctive dashboard design): stronger sources (Smashing Magazine, UX Collective/Prototypr) address design differentiation broadly rather than dashboards specifically; several corroborating accounts found during search (Medium opinion pieces on 'SaaS sameness') were judged too low-reliability to include as cited sources, so this step has real but less specific corroboration.

A few numeric claims surfaced during search (e.g. an uncited 'Microsoft research study' claiming hover states improve usability by 15%, and various colorblindness/contrast statistics from lower-tier accessibility-guide sites) could not be traced to a primary study and were excluded from sources.json rather than reported as fact — brief should avoid citing unverifiable statistics of this kind if they resurface.
summary: Gathered 28 sources across all eight research-plan steps in one round. Strong primary/authoritative coverage: Nielsen Norman Group (7 articles: dashboard preattentive processing/chart selection, progressive disclosure, F-shaped scanning, 10 usability heuristics, microinteractions, response-time limits, Gestalt proximity), WebAIM (WCAG contrast), Tink/Léonie Watson and amCharts (screen-reader/ARIA accessibility for tables and charts), Carbon Design System (IBM) and Material Design (Google) official design-system documentation, and Dan Saffer's foundational microinteractions framework. These are corroborated by credible design-practice publications (Pencil & Paper, Toptal, Smashing Magazine, UX Collective, Interaction Design Foundation, freeCodeCamp, The Data School on Tufte's chartjunk concept) plus a handful of lower-reliability but volume-corroborating trend/vendor blogs, clearly flagged as such in reliability_notes. Coverage spans IA (step 1), visual/dark-mode design (step 2), data-viz/chartjunk (step 3), interaction/microinteractions/empty-states/skeleton-screens (step 4), WCAG/ARIA accessibility (step 5), generic-vs-distinctive design (step 6, weaker), modern trends 2023-2026 (step 7, weaker), and anti-patterns/heuristics (step 8). All key claims in steps 1, 2, 3, 5, and 8 have multi-source, mostly primary-backed corroboration; steps 4, 6, and 7 have adequate but comparatively thinner corroboration, noted as gaps above rather than blocking a pass.
